About: The Astronomical and Terrestrial Telescope

Source

Topic
Geometric optics — refracting telescopes (Class 12, NCERT Ch. 9)
Simulation
Two refracting telescopes on one bench and one scale: the astronomical (Keplerian) pair, and the terrestrial version with an erecting lens between them.
Concept
You buy an erect image with tube LENGTH, not with magnification.
Serves
Angular magnification M = tan α′ / tan α = −fo/fe in normal adjustment; tube length fo + fe; the unit-magnitude erecting relay (u = v = 2f) and the terrestrial tube fo + 4f + fe; the intermediate real image; image inversion; the near-point form.
Inquiry
Predict — before dragging — which eyepiece magnifies more, and what the erecting lens actually costs.
Misconception
"A bigger eyepiece magnifies more" (fe is in the denominator), and "turning the image up must cost magnification" (it costs 4f of tube instead).

Guided Inquiry

1 · A star, and two lenses

A star is so far away that its light reaches the objective as a bundle of parallel rays, tilted by the angle α the star makes with the axis. The objective brings that bundle to a real image in its own focal plane, and the eyepiece — one focal length further on — sends the light out parallel again at a new angle α′. The angular magnification is M = tan α′ / tan α.

2 · Which eyepiece magnifies more?

The objective stays at fo = 1.00 m. Two eyepieces are available: one of focal length 50 mm, one of 20 mm. Which gives the larger angular magnification?

3 · The image arrives upside down

The emerging bundle leaves the eyepiece on the opposite side of the axis from the bundle that arrived, so the final image is inverted — that is the minus sign in M. A terrestrial telescope inserts a third converging lens of focal length f between objective and eyepiece, placed so it re-forms the intermediate image at the same size the other way up.

4 · What does the erecting lens cost?

The objective and the eyepiece keep the focal lengths they already had. What does adding the erecting lens cost?

5 · Why exactly 4f?

The erecting relay adds 4f, not 2f and not 6f. Which fact about a single thin lens fixes that number?

6 · The one thing to notice

Both telescopes magnify by the same amount: |M| = fo/fe. The only thing the erecting lens changes is the tube: 4f longer, and an image the right way up. Astronomers do not mind which way up a star field is, so they leave the lens out and keep the shorter tube; a spotting scope used on the ground puts it in and pays the length.

The other convention: the eyepiece is pushed in until the final image lands at the near point D = 25 cm, and the eye accommodates. Everything else on this page is the relaxed-eye normal adjustment, final image at infinity.

Angular magnification — the definition

M is a ratio of TANGENTS, not of angles. Using the angles themselves breaks as soon as α′ approaches 90°, which it does whenever fo/fe is large.

Astronomical telescope — normal adjustment

Both focal points coincide, so the system is afocal: parallel in, parallel out, final image at infinity and the eye relaxed. M < 0 — the final image is inverted.

Terrestrial telescope — the erecting relay

u = 2f is the one object distance a single lens images at unit magnitude, and it returns v = 2f with m = −1. That 2f + 2f is the whole extra tube, and it leaves |M| alone.

Near-point adjustment (the other convention)

Only if the eyepiece is pushed in so the final image lands at the near point D = 25 cm. The eye then accommodates. Everything drawn in the scene is the relaxed-eye normal adjustment above.

The Physics

The Astronomical and Terrestrial Telescope — Buying an Erect Image with Tube Length · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A refracting telescope uses two converging lenses. The objective gathers light from a distant object and makes a real image, and the eyepiece looks at that image. The sim also shows a third lens, which a terrestrial telescope adds.

What you'll learn

  • How two lenses turn a small viewing angle into a larger one.
  • What angular magnification means, and which way up the final image is.
  • What a third, erecting lens does to the image.
The apparatus. Light from a distant star arrives as parallel rays tilted at an angle α to the axis.

What's on screen

  • Objective: the blue lens at the left, labelled with its fo.
  • Erecting lens: the green lens, on the lower bench only.
  • Eyepiece: the pink lens, labelled with its fe.
  • Star's rays: the amber lines, with the real images drawn as small arrows.

The astronomical telescope is drawn on the upper bench and the terrestrial one below it. Both are drawn to one scale in metres.

03

The objective turns a star's light into a real image

A star is so far away that its light reaches the telescope as parallel rays. The whole bundle is tilted by the angle α the star makes with the axis. A converging lens brings parallel rays to a point in its focal plane, so the objective forms a small real image there.

The eyepiece sits one of its own focal lengths beyond that image. Light from the image then leaves the eyepiece as a parallel bundle again, now tilted at a new angle α′. Angular magnification compares the two tilts:

M = tan α′ / tan α
The definition: a ratio of tangents, not of angles.
  • The bundle is parallel to itself, not to the axis. That is why it focuses off the axis.
  • A ratio of tangents stays exact even when the emerging angle is large. A ratio of the angles themselves would not.
See itFollow one bundle across the upper bench. Watch for: parallel amber rays tilted at α on the left, a small arrow between the lenses, and a second parallel bundle leaving the eyepiece with the angle α′ marked.
04

The magnification is the ratio of the two focal lengths

A ray through the centre of the objective is not bent, so the real image has height h = fo tan α. The eyepiece sees that height from a distance fe, so tan α′ = h/fe. Dividing gives:

M = −fo/fe    L = fo + fe
Normal adjustment: the focal points coincide, so parallel light goes in and parallel light comes out.
  • At the opening values M = −1.00 m / 50 mm = −20.0, and the tube is L = 1.050 m.
  • The eyepiece focal length fe is in the denominator, so a shorter eyepiece magnifies more. With fe = 20 mm, M = −50.0.
  • Since tan α′ = 20 tan 2.5°, α′ = 41.1°. The angles are not in the ratio 20, because 20 × 2.5° would be 50°.

Because the final image is at infinity, the eye stays relaxed.

See itChange the eyepiece to fe = 20 mm. Watch for: Astronomical M = −50.0× in the readouts, α′ = 65.4° in the line of text under the upper bench, and tube L = 1.020 m.
05

The final image is upside down

The star lies above the axis, so its rays arrive descending. They cross at the real image, which therefore lies below the axis. The eyepiece then sends the bundle out rising, on the opposite side of the axis.

  • Traced backwards, the emerging rays seem to come from below the axis. The eye sees the star field inverted.
  • That is the minus sign in M = −fo/fe. The bundle leaves tilted the other way, so tan α′ is measured on the opposite side.
  • At the opening values the real image is fo tan 2.5° = 4.4 cm tall, drawn upside down, one fe before the eyepiece.

For stars this does not matter. No one knows which way up a star field should be.

See itReturn to the opening setup. Watch for: a small arrow below the axis labelled "real image ① — upside down, 4.4 cm tall", and the badge saying "minus: image INVERTED".
06

An erecting lens makes the image upright and costs tube length

A terrestrial telescope places a third converging lens, focal length f, between the objective and the eyepiece. It forms a second real image, the same size as the first and turned back up. The eyepiece then magnifies that upright image.

M = +fo/fe    L = fo + 4f + fe
The same magnitude of M, with the sign reversed. The tube is 4f longer.
  • At the opening values M = +20.0 and L = 1.450 m, against 1.050 m for the astronomical tube. The extra 4f is 0.400 m.
  • The relay hands on an image of equal height, so |M| is unchanged. Orientation is bought with length, not with magnification.
  • Astronomers leave the lens out and keep the shorter tube. A spotting scope used on the ground needs the upright view and pays the length.
See itRaise the erecting lens to f = 160 mm. Watch for: Extra tube = 4f reading +0.640 m, the lower tube growing to 1.690 m, and Terrestrial M still at +20.0×.
07

An object at 2f gives an image at 2f, the same size

The relay must make an image of unit size. For a thin lens the lens equation and the magnification are:

1/u + 1/v = 1/f    m = −v/u
Real-is-positive convention: u and v are distances in front of and behind the lens.
  • Eliminating v gives |m| = f/(u − f). Setting |m| = 1 gives u = 2f, and no other object distance works.
  • Then v = 2f and m = −1. The image is real, the same size and inverted relative to the first image, so it is upright overall.
  • The relay therefore takes 2f + 2f = 4f of tube. It is not 2f and not 6f.

With f = 120 mm, u = v = 240 mm and the extra tube is 0.480 m.

See itSet the erecting lens to f = 120 mm. Watch for: two labels u = 2f and v = 2f under a bracket reading 4f = 480 mm, and image ② as long as image ①.
08

Near-point adjustment gives a slightly larger magnification

Normal adjustment is the relaxed-eye setting drawn in the sim. A user may instead push the eyepiece in until the final image lies at the near point, D = 25 cm. The eye then has to accommodate.

MD = (fo/fe)(1 + fe/D)
Magnitude only. The factor 1 + fe/D is always above 1.
  • At the opening values MD = 20 × (1 + 0.05/0.25) = 24.0, against 20.0 in normal adjustment.
  • With fe = 20 mm the factor is 1.08, so MD = 54.0 against 50.0.
  • The gain is small for a short eyepiece. The benches still draw the normal adjustment.
See itSet fe to 20 mm and scroll to the last readout. Watch for: M, near-point adjustment at 54.0×, while the astronomical M above it stays −50.0×.
09

Summary

In one line. The objective makes a real image of a distant object, and the eyepiece sends that image out as a new parallel bundle at a different angle.

Key points

  • M = tan α′ / tan α = −fo/fe, with tube L = fo + fe.
  • An erecting lens gives M = +fo/fe and L = fo + 4f + fe, because the relay needs u = v = 2f.

Common mix-ups

  • "A longer eyepiece magnifies more." fe is in the denominator, so a shorter one does.
  • "Turning the image up must cost magnification." It costs 4f of tube instead.

Things to try on your own

  • Set the largest fo and the smallest fe, and read M. It is −75.0×.
  • Slide f and watch only the lower tube change, while both M values stay fixed.
